The failure is most likely caused by:

`org.joda.time.format.PeriodFormatterBuilder.FieldFormatter.parseInto(org.joda.time.ReadWritablePeriod, java.lang.String, int, java.util.Locale)`

Why:
- The failing input is `PT1003199059S`, which means the seconds field must parse the 10-digit value `1003199059`.
- `ISOPeriodFormat.standard()` builds the same formatter structure as the explicit builder used for `pfmt1`, so the bug is in how the appended formatter/parser is executed, not in the format definition itself.
- In `FieldFormatter.parseInto`, once it identifies the numeric token, it calls `parseInt(...)`.
- `parseInt(...)` explicitly switches to `Integer.parseInt(text.substring(...))` when `length >= 10`.
- For this test, the seconds token length is exactly 10, so this overflow-sensitive path is taken.
- That makes large-but-valid period values fail during parsing, which then bubbles up as the generic malformed-format exception thrown by `PeriodFormatter.parseMutablePeriod`.

Static evidence:
- `appendSecondsWithOptionalMillis()` uses a `FieldFormatter` for `SECONDS_OPTIONAL_MILLIS`.
- `FieldFormatter.parseInto` computes the numeric span and calls:
  - `setFieldValue(period, SECONDS, parseInt(text, position, length));`
- `FieldFormatter.parseInt` contains:
  - `if (length >= 10) return Integer.parseInt(text.substring(position, position + length));`

So the root cause is that period field parsing uses `int` parsing with an overflow-prone 10+ digit fast/slow path, and this rejects the regression input.

m29.content:
The failure is most likely caused by:

`org.joda.time.format.PeriodFormatterBuilder.FieldFormatter.parseInto(org.joda.time.ReadWritablePeriod, java.lang.String, int, java.util.Locale)`

Why:
- The failing input is `PT1003199059S`, which means the seconds field must parse the 10-digit value `1003199059`.
- `ISOPeriodFormat.standard()` builds the same formatter structure as the explicit builder used for `pfmt1`, so the bug is in how the appended formatter/parser is executed, not in the format definition itself.
- In `FieldFormatter.parseInto`, once it identifies the numeric token, it calls `parseInt(...)`.
- `parseInt(...)` explicitly switches to `Integer.parseInt(text.substring(...))` when `length >= 10`.
- For this test, the seconds token length is exactly 10, so this overflow-sensitive path is taken.
- That makes large-but-valid period values fail during parsing, which then bubbles up as the generic malformed-format exception thrown by `PeriodFormatter.parseMutablePeriod`.

Static evidence:
- `appendSecondsWithOptionalMillis()` uses a `FieldFormatter` for `SECONDS_OPTIONAL_MILLIS`.
- `FieldFormatter.parseInto` computes the numeric span and calls:
  - `setFieldValue(period, SECONDS, parseInt(text, position, length));`
- `FieldFormatter.parseInt` contains:
  - `if (length >= 10) return Integer.parseInt(text.substring(position, position + length));`

So the root cause is that period field parsing uses `int` parsing with an overflow-prone 10+ digit fast/slow path, and this rejects the regression input.

The dynamic verification tool was inconclusive due to debugger attachment failure, but the static code path aligns directly with the failing test and exception behavior.
